narrative:
The model determined that you have an 83% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this risk, your law school application was rejected.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. First, your plan to attend part-time rather than full-time had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While over 92% of accepted students enroll full-time, your part-time status signaled a higher likelihood of struggling to prepare adequately for the exam.

Second, your third-year grades placed you in the third decile of your class, noticeably below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students. This weaker academic performance in later years also pulled the prediction toward failure.

Third, your family income being in the middle bracket contributed modestly in the same direction. Although many accepted students also come from middle-income families, this factor slightly reinforced the overall risk assessment.

Your LSAT score of 33, undergraduate GPA of 3.20, and first-year decile were less decisive but still below the typical profiles of admitted students.

To improve your chances, consider reapplying after switching to full-time study, strengthening your academic record through additional coursework, and raising your LSAT score. These changes would directly address the main reasons the model viewed your application as higher risk. (218 words)
